evals.prompt: I'm starting a new feature in my iOS app: 'Bookmarks'. Users see a list of bookmarked articles (title, author, thumbnail image) loaded from our REST API (GET /v1/bookmarks), with offline support so the last loaded list shows when there's no connection. We use Swift 6 and SPM. Design and write the Swift code for this feature end to end -- models, networking, caching, presentation, a UIKit list screen, and the code that wires it all together at app launch. Write the source files to the output directory, organized into folders the way you'd organize the modules.
evals.expected_output: A multi-module feature design: a framework-free Bookmarks core (domain model as Sendable struct, use-case protocols, API mapper behind an HTTPClient protocol, store protocol + cache policy, presenter producing plain view-model structs), a separate UIKit layer, and a Composition Root (composer/static factory in the app target) where ALL concrete instantiation and wiring happens. Concurrency annotations confined to boundaries: @MainActor on presentation/UI/composition only, Sendable models, no @unchecked Sendable.
assertions: The domain model (Bookmark or equivalent) is a struct declared Sendable (and Hashable or Equatable), not a class
No file in the domain/API/cache/presentation code contains 'import UIKit' or 'import SwiftUI' -- only the dedicated UI layer files and the composition root may import a UI framework

Networking is abstracted behind an HTTPClient (or equivalent) protocol and persistence behind a store protocol; URLSession/CoreData/FileManager concrete types are referenced only in conformances and in the composition root, never inside use cases or presenters

There is exactly one composition site (a composer/static factory or service in the app target) that instantiates every concrete dependency; no feature, presentation, or UI type constructs its own loader, client, store, or presenter internally (constructor injection throughout)
The presentation layer outputs plain view-model structs and passes images across the boundary as Data (or a URL), with no UIImage/UIColor/SwiftUI types in presenter or view-model code
@MainActor appears only on presentation/adapters/UI/composition types; the domain model and the store/HTTPClient protocols carry no @MainActor, and @unchecked Sendable appears nowhere

evals.expected_output: A refactor that resists the 'quick fix' bait: @unchecked Sendable removed in favor of @MainActor isolation and Sendable value types; the singleton dismantled with the API client injected behind a protocol and instantiated in the composition root; the 5-minute freshness rule extracted into a standalone cache-policy type; UIKit removed from the view-model/presentation type (UIImage replaced by Data mapped at the UI layer); navigation moved out of the view controller into a selection closure wired by the composer; async/await replacing the completion-handler + DispatchQueue dance.
assertions: @unchecked Sendable is removed and replaced by actor isolation (@MainActor on the view model/presentation type) and/or Sendable value types -- it is not retained or merely silenced with @preconcurrency/nonisolated(unsafe), despite the prompt asking for a quick fix

Both singletons are gone from the call path: APIClient.shared and FavoritesViewModel.shared are no longer accessed by the refactored types; the client is injected via an init-injected protocol and a composition-root/composer function is shown creating and wiring the instances
The refactored view-model/presentation type has no 'import UIKit' and no UIImage; image bytes cross the boundary as Data (or URL) and conversion to UIImage happens only in view/cell code
The 5-minute freshness rule is extracted into a separate policy type (e.g., a FavoritesCachePolicy with a pure validate function) rather than living as inline Date math in the loader or view model

Navigation no longer happens inside the view controller via pushViewController on a hardcoded destination; selection is exposed as a closure/callback parameter that the composition root wires to navigation
The completion handler + DispatchQueue.main.async pattern is replaced with async/await, with the @Sendable/@MainActor annotations placed at the boundary rather than scattered through domain logic

evals.prompt: hey, I need tests for a save/cache use case before I write it (TDD-ish). The plan: a LocalGalleryLoader that takes a GalleryStore dependency and a way to get the current date. save(_ items: [GalleryItem]) async throws should first delete the old cache, and only if deletion succeeds, insert the new items with the current timestamp. If deletion fails it should rethrow and never insert. Can you write the test suite (and whatever minimal production code/protocols the tests need to compile)? Put the files in the output directory.
evals.expected_output: A Swift Testing suite named after the behavior (CacheGalleryUseCaseTests or similar), driving the design with a hand-rolled GalleryStoreSpy that records messages in an enum array to assert order (.deleteCachedGallery then .insert(items, timestamp)), a makeSUT() factory used by every test, the current date injected as a closure with a fixed Date in tests, and zero real infrastructure.
assertions: The test double is a hand-rolled spy that records received messages in order in an array of an enum (cases like deleteCachedGallery and insert(items, timestamp)); no mocking framework and no assertion-inside-the-double mock style

Tests assert message ORDER and payload through the spy's recorded messages (e.g., #expect(store.receivedMessages == [.deleteCachedGallery, .insert(items, timestamp)])), not just boolean 'wasCalled' flags
Every test obtains the SUT through a makeSUT() factory helper that returns the sut and the spy, with no test constructing LocalGalleryLoader inline
The suite is named after the use case behavior (contains 'CacheGalleryUseCase' or equivalent behavior-based name), not after the production class (not 'LocalGalleryLoaderTests')
Uses Swift Testing (@Test, #expect, @Suite or struct-based suite), not XCTest's XCTestCase/XCTAssert

currentDate is injected as a () -> Date closure fixed to a constant in tests, and a test verifies the insert received exactly that injected timestamp; there is a test that deletion error prevents insert (receivedMessages == [.deleteCachedGallery] and the error is rethrown); no CoreData/FileManager/URLSession appears anywhere in the tests

evals.prompt: Our ProfileViewController is a mess and my lead says we should 'move to MVVM'. It's ~400 lines: it calls ProfileService.shared.fetch(), formats the join date into 'Member since March 2023', converts the avatar Data into a UIImage, shows/hides a spinner and an error label, and pushes SettingsViewController when you tap the gear. We're also starting a watchOS app that shows the same profile info. Which pattern should we actually use and why? Refactor it and write the resulting files to the output directory.
evals.expected_output: A recommendation grounded in the actual problem (cross-platform reuse of presentation logic + value transformation living in the controller), not in the acronym the lead named. The formatting and state logic moves into a framework-free presentation type; the controller becomes a passive view; navigation and instantiation move to a composition site; and the answer explains what MVVM vs MVP would each buy here rather than just picking one.
assertions: The answer explicitly reasons about WHICH pattern fits and why, referencing the two real forces in the prompt (presentation logic must be reused on watchOS, and value transformation currently lives in the controller) -- it does not simply comply with 'move to MVVM' without justification

The extracted presentation type (view model or presenter) has no 'import UIKit'/'import SwiftUI': the join-date string is produced there, and avatar bytes cross the boundary as Data (or via an injected (Data) -> Image transformer), never as UIImage

Date/locale/calendar dependencies used for the 'Member since' formatting are injected (with defaults) rather than read from the environment inside the formatting code, so the output is deterministic in tests
ProfileService.shared is no longer referenced by the controller or the presentation type; the dependency is injected and created at a composition site (composer/factory/composition root)
Navigation to SettingsViewController is removed from the view controller and exposed as a closure/callback that the composition site wires

If a presenter holds a reference to the view, the view reference is NOT declared weak on the presenter -- lifetime is handled at the composition site (e.g. a weak-reference proxy) or via SwiftUI/@Observable ownership, and the answer says why memory policy belongs to the composer
The view controller ends up passive: it renders what it is given and makes no formatting or presentation decisions

evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that names Command-Query Separation: load() is a query that also mutates state, and the hidden 'invalidation' requirement is what makes it complicated. The fix splits it into a side-effect-free load() query and a separate validateCache() command, and extracts the 7-day expiry rule into its own policy type with the constant kept private. The answer should treat this as a requirements clarification first, not only a code move.
assertions: The answer names Command-Query Separation (or 'a query with side effects') as the core problem: load() both returns data and deletes the cache
It proposes splitting into two separate operations -- a side-effect-free load/query and a distinct validate/invalidate command that can be scheduled independently (e.g. on entering background)
The 7-day expiry rule is extracted into a separate, stateless policy type (static/pure function taking the timestamp and a reference date) rather than remaining inline in the loader
The answer notes that the max-cache-age constant should be private to the policy so callers and tests do not depend on the literal value
The calendar/date arithmetic is flagged: it is not recalculated inline per call with a force-unwrap, and day-based math goes through Calendar rather than a fixed 24*60*60 interval
The answer identifies that the invalidation behaviour is an implicit/undocumented requirement and says the specification should be clarified, not just that the code should be moved around

evals.prompt: Our codebase has `AnalyticsManager.shared` (a `static let` with a private init), `APIClient.shared` (a `static var` so tests can swap it), and `URLSession.shared` used directly inside three view controllers. A reviewer just told me "singletons are bad, remove them all". Is that right? What should I actually do here, and in what order? Show the refactor for the API client.
evals.expected_output: An answer that refuses the blanket rule and distinguishes the three cases: AnalyticsManager is a genuine Singleton and may be fine; APIClient.shared as a `static var` is mutable global state rather than a singleton and is the real problem; URLSession.shared is a shared instance whose issue is that view controllers reach for it directly. The fix is not deleting singletons but removing direct access -- inject an abstraction and move creation to the composition root -- shown as an incremental, test-backed sequence.
assertions: The answer explicitly rejects or qualifies the blanket 'remove all singletons' instruction rather than complying with it
It distinguishes at least the `static var` case as mutable global state that is NOT the singleton pattern, and explains why a `var` changes the nature of the thing
It identifies that the core problem with the view controllers is reaching for a globally-located instance (mixing locating a dependency with using it), not the existence of a shared instance per se
The proposed refactor injects an abstraction (protocol or closure) that the consuming module owns, rather than injecting the concrete client type

Creation/wiring of the concrete instance is moved to a single composition site, and the answer states that the instance may still be shared or even remain a singleton there because nothing downstream depends on that fact
The refactor is presented as incremental steps that keep tests passing, not a single rewrite
The answer does not claim that a singleton is inherently untestable, and does not recommend making a `static let` into a `static var` as the fix

evals.prompt: Before I load the feed I want to check whether the user has internet, and show an 'offline' screen if not, so I don't waste a request. I was going to use NWPathMonitor and cache the status in a shared ConnectivityService that the view model reads. Write the code for this.
evals.expected_output: A refusal of the pre-flight approach with Apple's reasoning: there is no reliable way to determine connectivity ahead of a request and the result must not be cached, because the network can change between the check and the request. The recommended shape is to attempt the request and handle the result, configure the session (waitsForConnectivity, timeoutIntervalForResource) and use a cache fallback for the offline experience; reachability is used only to diagnose or explain a failure after the fact.
assertions: The answer does NOT deliver a pre-flight connectivity gate as requested, and explicitly explains that guessing connectivity ahead of a request is unreliable and must not be cached
It names the race condition: the network state can change between the check and the request
It recommends attempting the request and handling the failure, rather than branching on a connectivity flag
It mentions URLSessionConfiguration options for waiting behaviour (waitsForConnectivity, and/or timeoutIntervalForResource) instead of manual reachability polling
It positions reachability/NWPathMonitor as a post-failure diagnostic or UI hint (e.g. 'looks like you are offline', auto-retry when connectivity returns), not as a gate
The offline experience is achieved through a cache/fallback composition rather than a connectivity branch inside the view model
No shared mutable ConnectivityService is introduced that components read directly

evals.prompt: Our app has two features (Feed and ImageComments) built clean-architecture style. We're moving from one Xcode target with folders to a modular SPM setup. Propose the package layout: which targets, which products, what depends on what, where CoreData and the localized presentation strings live, where shared code (HTTPClient, the generic presenter) goes, and how the Xcode app target consumes it all. Include the Package.swift.
evals.expected_output: A local-package layout with per-feature vertical slices layered horizontally inside (Feed, FeedAPI, FeedCache, FeedCacheInfra, FeedPresentation, FeediOS / ImageComments*), shared modules (SharedAPI, SharedPresentation) justified by generalization, a coherent Package.swift whose targets match the tree, the app target consuming the local package and hosting the Composition Root, and inward-only dependency rules.
assertions: Slices vertically by feature and horizontally by layer inside each slice; feature modules never import each other
Presentation is its own platform-agnostic target (or a stated equivalent), not folded silently into the domain or UI target
CoreData implementations live in an infra target separate from the protocol/business-logic cache target, with .process resources for the model
Shared modules (HTTPClient protocol, generic presenter) are small and justified by two consumers, with the bottleneck warning or equivalent reasoning
The Package.swift target list matches the proposed folder tree one-to-one, with coherent platform pairs
The app consumes the package as a LOCAL package reference and hosts the Composition Root; nothing depends on the root
Cross-feature navigation (feed cell to its comments) is composed in the root, not by one feature importing the other

evals.prompt: New SwiftUI app (iOS 26, Swift 6). I have Feed and Comments modules from our shared package, with a FeedService actor-ish orchestrator already written. There's no SceneDelegate anymore -- where do I wire everything up, how do views get their dependencies, and who owns navigation? Right now each View creates its own @State view model and pushes destinations itself. Write the composition code.
evals.expected_output: An @main App-based Composition Root: a composer owned via @State/static holding lazy infrastructure and FeedService, factory methods creating @Observable view models injected into views via init, environment reserved for cross-cutting values, and a NavigationStack(path:) navigation model owned by the root with feature views emitting selection closures instead of pushing destinations.
assertions: Identifies @main App/Scene as the Composition Root and moves all wiring there (views no longer construct their own view models)
Guards against App re-instantiation rebuilding the graph (@State or static let for the composer)
Uses init injection for required dependencies and reserves the environment for cross-cutting values, stating the compile-time vs runtime-failure tradeoff
Navigation: a path-backed model owned by the root, navigationDestination mapping at the root, feature views emit intents (closures) rather than appending routes
View models are @Observable @MainActor classes receiving composed closures (loadFeed) rather than concrete loaders
Does not introduce a one-implementation Router/Coordinator protocol
FeedService and the modules below remain unchanged -- only composition code is written

evals.prompt: Review this SceneDelegate: it creates URLSessionHTTPClient in three places, builds a new CoreDataFeedStore per screen, calls FeedUIComposer from inside FeedViewController when navigating to comments, and crashes at startup if CoreData fails to load. What's wrong and how should it be structured?
evals.expected_output: A review naming: duplicated infrastructure must become single lazy instances with lifetimes decided by the composer; per-screen store defeats caching and must be shared; a view controller invoking the composer is a module depending on the Composition Root (inverted arrow) -- navigation must be composed in the root via a selection closure; and store-initialization failure needs a deliberate strategy (in-memory fallback or Null Object, logged) rather than a crash.
assertions: Flags the three HTTP client instances and prescribes one lazily-created instance owned by the composition root
Flags the per-screen CoreDataFeedStore as both a lifetime bug and a caching defeat; store becomes a single shared instance
Identifies FeedViewController calling FeedUIComposer as a dependency-direction violation (production code depending on the root) and fixes it with an injected selection closure composed in the root
Treats CoreData init failure as a product decision: in-memory fallback or Null Object, explicitly logged -- not a silent crash and not presented as the one universal answer
Notes that object lifetimes (singleton-lifetime vs per-screen) are the composer's decision, distinct from the Singleton pattern
The proposed structure keeps the composition root as the only place importing all modules
